displayQuote: Only the dead have seen the end of war

meta.title: Who really said "Only the dead have seen the end of war"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Plato. George Santayana wrote it in Soliloquies in England (1922); Gen. MacArthur mislabeled it 'Plato' in his 1962 West Point speech.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Only the dead have seen the end of war'?
meta.ogDescription: It's found nowhere in Plato. The real author is George Santayana, in his 1922 soliloquy 'Tipperary' — MacArthur popularized the Plato myth in 1962.

answer.label: Not Plato — actually George Santayana
answer.sourceLine: The line is not in Plato — scholars cannot find it in any dialogue, and Plato expert Nathan Tarcov told fact-checkers “it just doesn’t sound to me like Plato.” It was written by George Santayana in his soliloquy “Tipperary,” published in Soliloquies in England ↗ (1922): “Only the dead are safe; only the dead have seen the end of war.” The Plato attribution was popularized after Gen. Douglas MacArthur attributed it to him in his 1962 West Point address.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Soliloquies in England and Later Soliloquies
Gen. Douglas MacArthur, 1962 West Point farewell address

source.excerpt: Yet the poor fellows think they are safe! They think that the war — perhaps the last of all wars — is over! Only the dead are safe; only the dead have seen the end of war.
trail: A University of Chicago fact-check traces the line to Santayana’s 1922 Soliloquies in England and quotes Plato scholar Nathan Tarcov that it is not Plato’s (CheckYourFact ↗).
A Plato-studies FAQ places the sentence in the soliloquy “Tipperary” and notes it appears nowhere in Plato’s dialogues (dialogues-de-platon.org ↗).
Wikiquote ↗ lists the line among Santayana’s sourced quotations, tied to Soliloquies in England.
source.excerptNote: The popular one-line version drops Santayana’s preceding clause, “Only the dead are safe.”

source.rightsNote: The line first appeared in Soliloquies in England and Later Soliloquies, published in 1922 by Constable and Scribner. A U.S. work published before 1931 is in the public domain; Santayana himself died in 1952.

author.name: George Santayana
author.heading: Who was George Santayana?
author.bio: George Santayana (born Jorge Agustín Nicolás Ruiz de Santayana in Madrid) was a philosopher, essayist and poet who wrote entirely in English and taught at Harvard before settling in Europe. His Soliloquies in England (1922) collected reflections written in Britain during and just after the First World War. He is also the source of the far more famous aphorism “Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.”

misattribution.heading: The Plato mix-up
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most persistent fake “Plato” quotes on the internet — carved on war memorials and dropped into films, yet found nowhere in Plato.

items.why: The sentence appears in none of Plato’s dialogues; scholars including the University of Chicago’s Nathan Tarcov reject it as inconsistent with his style (CheckYourFact ↗).
MacArthur quoted the line as Plato’s in his 1962 “Duty, Honor, Country” address at West Point, cementing the false attribution (dialogues-de-platon.org ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The words are George Santayana’s, written in the soliloquy “Tipperary” in Soliloquies in England (1922), where they read “Only the dead are safe; only the dead have seen the end of war” (Wikiquote ↗).

context.heading: Why it sounds ancient
lead: Santayana wrote “Tipperary” while living in England during the First World War, watching soldiers celebrate what they hoped was “the last of all wars.” His grim rejoinder — that only the dead ever escape war — has an aphoristic, classical cadence, which is precisely why it slid so easily onto Plato.

The attribution hardened when Gen. Douglas MacArthur cited it as Plato’s in 1962. From there it spread to the wall of the Imperial War Museum and to the 2001 film Black Hawk Down, each repetition lending the misattribution more authority.
